reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / movement disorder literature
clinicalPearls: A segmental cranial dystonia combining blepharospasm with oromandibular dystonia affecting the jaw, tongue and lower face
Blepharospasm causes involuntary forced eyelid closure that can be functionally blinding
Oromandibular dystonia produces involuntary jaw opening or closing, lip and tongue movements, and can impair speech and eating
It typically begins in mid to late adult life and is more common in women
Sensory tricks (geste antagoniste) such as touching the face may transiently relieve the spasms
Botulinum toxin injection into the affected muscles is the mainstay of treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Meige syndrome is a focal or segmental dystonia of the cranial muscles arising from dysfunction within basal ganglia motor circuits and their control of facial and jaw musculature. As in other dystonias, abnormal patterns of muscle co-contraction produce sustained or repetitive involuntary movements, and altered sensorimotor integration underlies both the dystonic postures and the benefit from sensory tricks. Most cases are idiopathic, though secondary cranial dystonia can follow certain drug exposures or brain lesions.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic combination of signs
Medication history to identify drug-induced tardive syndromes
MRI of the brain if features suggest a secondary cause
Assessment of functional impact on vision, speech and eating
Evaluation for sensory tricks supporting a dystonic diagnosis
redFlags: Rapid progression or additional neurological signs suggesting secondary dystonia
reference.prognosis: The condition is usually chronic, but repeated botulinum toxin treatment provides substantial symptomatic relief for most patients and can preserve function.
pitfalls: Mistaking bilateral cranial dystonia for unilateral hemifacial spasm
Overlooking a tardive syndrome from previous neuroleptic exposure
Underestimating the functional impact of severe blepharospasm
Failing to recognise sensory tricks that confirm dystonia
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Inject botulinum toxin into the affected periocular and oromandibular muscles as the mainstay of treatment
Use oral agents such as anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, baclofen or tetrabenazine for adjunctive or wider symptom control
Encourage sensory tricks (geste antagoniste) that transiently relieve the spasms
Review and withdraw causative drugs where a tardive or drug-induced cranial dystonia is identified
Consider deep brain stimulation of the globus pallidus for severe, refractory disease
Provide supportive measures for vision, speech and swallowing with multidisciplinary neurology, ophthalmology and speech therapy input
